title: Asking and accepting
hookLine: Ardas both asks and then accepts the answer

cards: The end of a gurdwara service. Everyone stands, hands joined, faces turned toward the Guru Granth Sahib, and one person leads the Ardas, the standing petition, while the sangat listens.
Names are spoken: someone in the hospital, a new baby, a family about to travel, a student with an exam.
Then the asking ends, everyone bows, and a reading is taken from the Granth, the hukamnama, received as the Guru's word for the day. First the asking. Then the listening.

teach.b: First, Ardas really asks. It names needs and sorrows, journeys and exams, the sick and the grieving, and it ends by asking for the good of all. Sikhs aren't asked to pretend they need nothing.

Second, it asks humbly. Near the close, the one leading asks forgiveness for any mistakes made, bhul chuk, even in the prayer itself. And some sangats recite a verse from Guru Arjan's Sukhmani Sahib just before the Ardas.
In paraphrase: you are the master, to you this prayer; body and soul are your gift; you are mother and father, we are your children.
The one asking stands like a child before a parent, not a customer at a counter. Third, it accepts.
The prayer ends with the will: tere bhaane sarbat da bhala, by your will, the good of all. Then the hukam is read and received as the Guru's word, whatever it says.
Two open hands: lifted up to ask, and left open for whatever comes down. Fourth, a look back.
This week the thieves came through one by one: pride, attachment, greed, desire.
Then chardi kala, rising spirits rooted in the Name, and acceptance and rising together. And now the Ardas, which holds all of it. The thieves grab.
The Ardas asks, and then lets go.

how: Sikhs offer Ardas standing with joined hands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the close of services and before important tasks; afterward a hukamnama is read from the Granth and received as the Guru's word for the day.

o: asking only for what you're sure God will give
accepting everything so you never need to ask
asking plainly, then receiving whatever answer comes

games.q: asking and accepting: tap the pairs.
p: the Guru's word for the day
you are the master, to you this prayer

s: the Ardas only praises and never asks for anything
it names real needs: the sick, travelers, exams, and the good of all.
after the Ardas, a reading is taken from the Granth
the hukamnama, received as the Guru's word for the day.

games.q: you've stood and asked, with your whole heart, for something you badly want. the answer seems to be no. what does the shape of the Ardas point toward?
o: keep asking louder until it changes.
accept the answer, and keep your hands open.
games.why: the Ardas asks plainly, then closes with tere bhaane, by your will, and the hukam that follows is received whatever it says.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you want, for yourself or for someone you love, and say it once, plainly, inside, the way the Ardas names real needs; if you pray, offer it as your petition.
Then set it down, the way the sangat bows when the Ardas ends. If it comes back, notice it, and set it down again.

wordCard.voice: Asking and accepting. The Ardas names real needs plainly, closes with the will, and then listens to the Guru's word, whatever it says. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the standing petition Sikhs offer to close a service or begin a task.

carryVoice: Your line: ask, then accept. Two open hands, lifted and then waiting. A week of thieves and trust, done.

sources.ref: Ardas and the taking of the hukam
Ang 268 (Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan: tu thakur tum peh ardaas)
